metadata.section: Chapter 9: Zeng et al.'s E Test
metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits

blocks.content: A variant of the H test was proposed by Zeng et al. (2006), who noted that the most powerful contrasts between regions of the unfolded frequency spectrum following selection should involve high- versus low-frequency sites. However, most contrasts involve a comparison with $ _ II $, which is a measure of intermediate-frequency alleles. To rectify this, Zeng et al. introduced the estimator, $ _L $, based on a weight, $ c_i = i $, that places more emphasis on high-frequency sites than $ _S $ (but not as much as $ _H $). For these weights, Equation 9.23b implies $ h(n) = n - 1 $, and hence Equation 9.23c yields [[SEE_FORMULA:9.28a]]
Zeng et al.'s E test contrasts the high- and low-frequency regions of the frequency spectrum, [[SEE_FORMULA:9.28b]] where [[SEE_FORMULA:9.28c]]

Again the variance is approximated by replacing $ \theta $ and $ \theta^{2} $ with their estimates from Equation 9.21b. A negative E indicates an excess of low- versus high-frequency sites relative to expectations of the equilibrium neutral model. This occurs immediately after a sweep, as the excess of high-frequency alleles is quickly lost by drift (due to their fixation), while at the same time mutation is generating an excess of low-frequency sites, which have yet to drift up to their neutral equilibrium values. The unique feature of E is its ability to yield a signal after a sweep, which can persist up to $ 2 N_{e} $ generations (and hence much longer than H).
